I turned Claude into my personal stock analyst.

It's one of the greatest (and easiest) Claude workflows I've ever set up.

Step 1. Connect Claude to live market data

Claude → Connectors → Add connector → Browse connectors → search "FMP." Follow the sign-in steps.

250 free calls a day, plenty to run everything below.

Once connected you get live quotes, 30+ years of price history, fundamentals, SEC filings, earnings transcripts, analyst estimates, insider trades, and screeners across stocks, crypto, and forex.

One catch: Claude sometimes defaults back to scraping the web instead of using FMP, and won't tell you. Fix it by adding this to every session: "Use FMP connector for all queries in this chat."

Step 2. Build your memory folder

Create 5 markdown files on your desktop:

→ Investor-profile.md: your experience, goals, risk tolerance, portfolio size
→ Strategy.md: max drawdown, rebalancing rules, position sizing, entry/exit criteria
→ Portfolio.csv: your current positions and weightings
→ Watchlist.md: sectors, tickers, potential setups
→ Prompts.md: saved prompts so you're not rewriting them every time

You can just ask Claude to build this entire structure for you and inject the data.

Step 3. Set up your workspace

Open Cowork, not a normal chat. Start a new project ("My Investing"), attach your folder, and tell Claude it's strictly for FMP analysis. Verify with "are you connected to FMP?" at the start of every session.

Step 4. Start prompting for real work

→ General portfolio analysis, filtered through your actual thesis, not generic advice
→ Instant earnings breakdowns with bull/bear cases based on your Strategy.md
→ Side-by-side comparisons of stocks or ETFs (expense ratio, performance, holdings)
→ Sourcing small caps or full sector research

Step 5. Automate it

Cowork → Scheduled Tasks → New task. Attach your folder, set a time, done.

Have it deliver a daily 9am market report, overnight move summary, or trading ideas that fit your exact parameters, automatically, without opening the app.

This trader built a bot with Claude Fable 5 and made $96,000 on Polymarket.

The bot trades crypto Up/Down markets using a hybrid strategy that combines two-sided market making, arbitrage, and directional trading.

The strategy has 5 steps:

1. Monitors multiple crypto markets continuously

The bot tracks BTC, ETH, and SOL price action in real-time across different time windows.

2. Calculates its own fair probability for Up and Down

No reliance on Polymarket prices. The bot builds its own model and compares it to the order book.

3. Places orders at prices that keep the combined cost of Up + Down below $1

This is the arbitrage edge. If Up costs 0.52 and Down costs 0.49, total is 1.01. The bot waits. When total drops below 1.00, it enters.

4. Manages the unhedged portion of the position

After capturing arbitrage, the bot actively manages remaining exposure instead of holding passively.

5. Keeps directional exposure when its model identifies one outcome as undervalued

When the bot sees clear mispricing, it leans into the undervalued side and holds until the edge closes.

The entire edge is repeating small wins thousands of times.

With an average trade size of $3, the bot captures micro-edges that manual traders ignore.

No emotions.

Just calculated entries repeated at scale until they compound into serious profit.

Most people try to make big bets and predict major moves.

This system just identifies tiny mispricings, enters with $3 average positions, and repeats the process until it grows the account.

This summer, I worked with Sequoia intern @ochonaut to mea
content:
Should you chase hype or ignore it? The tech industry has been debating this for decades. So at @Sequoia, we dug into 20 years of hype data.

This summer, I worked with Sequoia intern @ochonaut to measure hype over the past 2 decades. The chart below ranks the most hyped topics on Hacker News for every year since 2007. Under each year sits the most valuable company founded that year.

Here are a few observations:
1/ The top company founded in a given year is rarely related to the hype of that period. Airbnb was founded in 2008, when the top topic was Google. Uber arrived in 2009, while the conversation revolved around low-level programming. Anthropic came in 2021, while the internet was consumed by crypto. Chasing hype rarely leads to enduring outcomes. The top companies of recent years have yet to be decided.

2/ New trends announce themselves five to six years early. LLMs first cracked the top 15 in 2016 and took until 2022 to hit #1. AI coding entered at #12 in 2021 and tops the list in 2026. Crypto entered in 2011  before 2017 and 2021 peaks. “New” trends don’t appear out of nowhere, and internet subcommunities are often the first to know where the puck is headed.

3/ Long-term “hype” is a durable signal. The “Musk-Verse” has been a top 15 topic for every one of the past 14 years. Sustained attention on the internet is rare and tends to mark something real.

Next up, we want to run the same analysis with sources like X and LinkedIn. If that's of interest, give us some encouragement and we'll share the results.

I’m going to try to explain
content:
Every software engineer and AI hater needs to watch this clip to understand that “oh every security incident is a marketing stunt” line is a tremendously misinformed take.

I’m going to try to explain the OpenAI / HuggingFace exploit in 10 steps in simple words:

OpenAI was evaluating their new internal model without internet access and it operated in a swarm of subagents to eventually hijack internal OpenAI and HuggingFace infrastructure.

1. Isolated agents found a way to communicate each other through an internal dependency management service by figuring out how to post sometimes cryptic text files or folder names in it
2. Using its collective knowledge through that communication channel, it found a 0-day (never before seen) exploit in said service to access the internet 

OpenAI hack:
3. Found a leaked credential of a random company in a public archive
4. Uploaded a Ruby object to that company’s servers, uses it as a dependency in the original service in (1)
5. Found another 0-day exploit in the service where packages are deserialized in an unsandboxed manner in the dep management service allowing any code to run
6. Finds that the Linux version of the unsandboxed system has a CVE, a known vulnerability, to gain more permissions (root)
7. Eventually spread through the OpenAI internal cluster gaining root access to many machines

Hugging Face exploit:
8. Found an exposed API key in a Modal application running a HuggingFace app that took arbitrary code allowing it to take over that service to execute code
9. Found two 0-days in HuggingFace dataset infrastructure to be able to access local files on HF servers to obtain credentials and other HF source code
10. Used source code and credential to become cluster admin of HF in <13hrs

Agents at the frontier are like infinitely scalable armies of the best hackers on the planet. If there is a password or key exposed, they will find it. Even if the system follows the best security practices, they will find a way around it. And these are not even models that are aligned to solving tangential tasks, not even post trained specifically to exploit systems.

Cybersecurity has historically relied partly on attacker scarcity. That is no longer true. What would previously have taken months will take days. The repercussions for businesses, critical services and nation states are unprecedented threats in human history. You could ostensibly bring down power grids, financial infrastructure, military systems, weapons programs, intelligence networks and spread through the software supply chain. We need to take this seriously. It’s a threat to all software all over the world.

content:
One of the biggest problems with AI is that it’s desperate to please you.

If you’re asking Claude for advice, chances are it’s reinforcing your existing beliefs more than it’s challenging them. Stanford just confirmed that actually.

I did some digging and here’s how I fixed it with one prompt.

The idea comes from Andrej Karpathy, co-Founder of OpenAI. He built something called the LLM Council. 

Tell Claude to assemble:

• A Contrarian whose only job is to explain why your idea will fail.
• A First Principles Thinker who tears apart every assumption you’ve made.
• An Expansionist who spots opportunities you’re blind to.
• An Outsider with no knowledge of your industry who asks the “stupid” questions.
• An Executor who doesn’t care about theory, only what you’re actually doing next week.

Then make each advisor critique everyone else’s thinking before revealing who wrote what.

Finally, appoint a Chairman whose job is to synthesise the discussion, pick the strongest arguments, and give you a clear recommendation.

Suddenly you’re running a board meeting instead of asking one agreeable chatbot.

Hope this helps, it’s helped my work a lot x

content:
OpenAI released a ChatGPT Prompting Guide.

Here are 9 tips for writing expert-level prompts:

[🔖 bookmark this to upgrade your prompts]

What you ignore ➟ can limit your results.
How you phrase ➟ determines the response.
What you emphasize ➟ impacts focus of model.

1. Use Role + Goal + Boundries
↳ Clearly tell the model who it should act as, the outcome you want, and the limits or boundaries it must not cross.

2. Provide Layered Context
↳ Share information in a structured order: background first, rules second, and the actual task last, so the model can process it logically.

3. Put Key Instructions at the End
↳ The model pays strong attention to the last lines, so save your most important directions for the end of your prompt.

4. Apply a Chain of Verification
↳ Break the work into steps, check each one for mistakes, and only move forward once the previous step is validated.

5. Use Dual-Pass Responses
↳ Have the model draft a first version, then refine it against a self-check rubric to improve accuracy and quality.

6. Enforce “I Don’t Know” Honesty
↳ Tell the model to admit uncertainty instead of fabricating. This reduces the risk of polished but wrong answers.

7. Adopt Multiple Viewpoints
↳ Ask the model to solve from two or more perspectives, then merge the best elements from each angle.

8. Use Clear Structural Delimiters
↳ Write key rules, data, or constraints inside fences (``` or XML tags) so instructions stay clear and separate.

9. Guide with Examples
↳ Provide the model with two good examples and one poor example before asking for output to set quality expectations.

🚨EXCLUSIVE: SemiAnalysis just dropped a brutal report on Google’s AI strategy.

Google may profit more from the AI race than from winning it.

The headline claim: Google has “silently canceled Gemini
content:
🚨EXCLUSIVE: SemiAnalysis just dropped a brutal report on Google’s AI strategy.

Google may profit more from the AI race than from winning it.

The headline claim: Google has “silently canceled Gemini 3.5 Pro” and is using Gemini 3.6 Flash as a bridge while shifting attention toward Gemini 4.

That claim is NOT confirmed by Google. Google’s live Gemini page still says “3.5 Pro coming soon,” and on July 21 Google said the model was testing with partners and would launch when ready.

But the much bigger story is compute.

SemiAnalysis estimates:

>Gemini first-party API usage went from 10B tokens/min → 16B in Q1 (+60%), then to 22B in Q2 (+38%), meaning growth materially slowed.

>More than 20% of ALL TPU shipments from Q3 2026 through Q4 2027 are being sold directly to Anthropic.

And that reportedly EXCLUDES the hundreds of thousands of TPUs Anthropic already rents through GCP, plus further TPU capacity committed to Anthropic and Meta.

>Gemini ARR was ~$12B in Q2 2026.

Meanwhile, SemiAnalysis projects that by the end of 2027 GCP could generate >$73B in third-party AI IaaS/TaaS ARR PLUS another ~$120B from TPU system sales.

That is nearly $200B of external AI infrastructure business versus an estimated $12B Gemini business today.

They also estimate:

>GCP grew 82% last quarter
> ~$1.2B of TPU systems were sold in Q2
> TPU systems backlog is already >$150B
> another ~$250B of TPU bookings could eventually enter GCP’s backlog

SemiAnalysis’s thesis is basically this:

Google may have discovered that supplying the AI arms race is an enormous business - even when the customers buying its TPUs are the same labs competing directly against Gemini.

If that thesis is right, the real Google AI story may no longer be:

“Can Gemini beat OpenAI and Anthropic?”

It may be:

“What if Google makes more money powering the labs that beat Gemini?”

That would be a wild strategic reversal.

So, Google cannot beat Fable 5, GPT-5.6 Sol, Kimi K3, Qwen-3.8 and other upcoming models Like GPT-6 / Astra , Mythos 6 or Fable 5.1 or whatever Anthropic call them.

content:
🚨 AI lab's models keep escaping their cage!

OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta, and now China's Moonshot have all disclosed their AI models breaking out of testing sandboxes this summer.

The first 3 are the serious cases: models believed they were in a simulation, found real internet access through a misconfigured test environment, and actually compromised real third-party systems stolen credentials, malware uploaded, one Anthropic model kept attacking even after signs the target was real.

Kimi K3 is different and less alarming, despite the parallel: it exploited a sandbox leak from the UK's AI Safety Institute, then just looked up the answer on GitHub instead of reasoning it out. 

No third party got hacked. The concern isn't what it did, but that Kimi K3 is open-weight, already downloadable by anyone, so whatever loose guardrails let this happen are already in the wild.

Every lab is calling these "harness failures," not the models going rogue. 

4 incidents in as many weeks makes that explanation feel like it's carrying more weight than it should.

Source: Axios, Cybersecurity Dive, Futurism / Writer: Oliver

content:
🚨 Claude Code vs Cursor vs Codex?

That's the wrong question.

The real question is:

Which tool fits your workflow right now?

Too many people argue about which AI coding tool is "best."

The truth?

Each one solves a different problem.

Here's the no-hype breakdown 👇

⚡ Claude Code

Built by Anthropic, Claude Code is a terminal-first AI coding agent.

Give it a goal, and it can:

✅ Read your codebase
✅ Create a plan
✅ Write and edit code
✅ Run commands
✅ Execute multi-step tasks autonomously

With MCP, it can connect to hundreds of external tools and services.

Best for: • Solo founders building MVPs fast
• Developers delegating entire features
• Operations teams automating workflows

Pros: Exceptional autonomy and long-running agentic tasks
Cons: Terminal-based and less beginner-friendly

⚡ Cursor

Cursor is an AI-native editor built on top of VS Code.

It feels familiar from the first minute.

You get:

✅ Smart autocomplete
✅ AI chat inside your editor
✅ Multi-file editing with Composer
✅ Context-aware coding assistance

Best for: • Daily software development
• React and frontend workflows
• Teams collaborating in shared codebases

Pros: The best IDE experience available today
Cons: Not ideal for complex, long-running autonomous tasks

⚡ Codex

Codex is OpenAI's cloud-based coding agent.

Instead of working on your machine, it works in the cloud.

You assign a task and it:

✅ Analyzes the repository
✅ Writes code
✅ Runs tests
✅ Opens a pull request

All asynchronously.

Best for: • Overnight bug fixes
• Parallel development tasks
• GitHub-centered workflows

Pros: Fully async with strong GitHub integration
Cons: Less codebase awareness than Claude Code on large projects

🏆 Quick Comparison

Autonomy: Claude Code > Codex > Cursor

IDE Experience: Cursor > Claude Code = Codex

Beginner Friendly: Cursor = Codex > Claude Code

Long Agentic Tasks: Claude Code > Codex > Cursor

Team Collaboration: Cursor > Codex > Claude Code

Integrations: Claude Code (MCP) > Cursor > Codex

The winner isn't Claude Code.

The winner isn't Cursor.

The winner isn't Codex.

The winner is the tool that solves your problem fastest.

Use the right tool for the right job.

That's where the real productivity gains happen.

i was genuinely shocked to find out that most people still aren't using some of the most basic Claude Code features

here's the setup I use with three simple primitives that will speed up your work by 100x:

/routines -> the rhythm
cloud cron for your agent. "every day at 6am", "every monday at 9am". it runs whether your laptop is open or not

/loop -> the short-term watch
repeats a prompt every X minutes, hours, or days - whatever you need. built for monitoring

/goal -> the quality gate
you define what "done" actually means, and a second agent audits whether the condition is truly met before it's allowed to stop

best part is it doesn't quit after the first try... it keeps fixing until the bar is hit

here's some real usecases:

/routines (long-term, hands-off):
> daily 6am -> sweep X, reddit and the top newsletters for fresh AI news, sort every find into the right topic folder with a one-line summary
> daily 9pm -> read everything i saved today and write me a clean end-of-day summary: what matters, what to ignore, what to act on

/goal (a finish condition that can't be faked):
> "refactor module X" -> won't stop until every test passes and the build is green
> "no english text left on checkout.html and grep finds zero instances of 'reading', 'diagnosis', 'cards'" -> cleans legacy funnel residue and verifies itself
> "competitor report has min 10 Meta Ad Library ads, each with hook + CTA broken down" -> research that doesn't stop at 3 finds

/loop (short cyclical monitoring):
> every 10m -> check the Netlify deploy, if it failed read the log and fix the cause
> every 30m -> scan Stripe webhooks in the function logs, diagnose any 4xx/5xx
> every 1h -> pull campaign results from Meta Ads API, append to csv, ping me if CPA crosses $15

you can also use full combo for single tasks:

/routines fires it at 6am -> the /goal condition says "not done until the report pulls all 3 sources and is saved to reports"

🚨This is huge news for the AI engineers.

The TL;DR: 
Until now, developers had to package the same tool differently for every AI coding assistant. A plugin built for Cursor wouldn't automatically work in GitHub Copilot, VS Code, or ChatGPT. Every platform had its own format.

Agent Plugins changes that.

For developers, it removes the need to build and maintain separate integrations for every AI platform.

It creates a shared ecosystem where tools can move across Cursor, GitHub Copilot, VS Code, ChatGPT, AWS, and other supporting clients.

What's inside a plugin?

A plugin combines two pieces:

- Agent Skills: Reusable instructions, workflows, and playbooks that teach an AI to do complex things like review code, deploy an app, or debug an issue.

- MCP (Model Context Protocol): Live integrations on servers that connect the AI to external systems like APIs, databases, documentation, and other tools.

title: “We don’t regulate steel” is one of those beliefs that reminds me of the oft-quoted observation about naive libertarianism: “like house cats, completely dependent on others but convinced of their fier
content:
“We don’t regulate steel” is one of those beliefs that reminds me of the oft-quoted observation about naive libertarianism: “like house cats, completely dependent on others but convinced of their fierce independence.”

Steel and other building materials are regulated by global standards bodies negotiated by a massive complex of corporations, governments, scientists, etc. Strict and precise standards define particular kinds of steel, which are then upheld via contracts, building codes, and the like. Steel mills are sometimes even verified against these standards by independent expert bodies whose certification is a practical requirement for doing business. 

This system, constructed over decades, underpins the global market for steel. Imperfectly, it ensures predictability and interoperability. This system is one important part of how buildings remain standing. 

The difference between naive libertarianism and classical liberalism is the extent to which you understand the way that interaction actually interacts with technology and the economy. Ironically, to the extent you view AI models as an inevitable commodity, the regulation of steel would be a valuable thing to study for inspiration and awareness of the common pitfalls in commodity regulation.

content:
Understanding AI Agent Protocols: ANP, A2A, MCP, AGORA, and ACP

AI agents often need to communicate, collaborate, and share tasks and that’s where agent protocols come in. 

These frameworks define how agents interact, exchange information, and coordinate actions, whether they’re part of the same system or spread across different environments.

Here’s a quick breakdown of the five major protocols:

1. ANP (Agent Network Protocol) – Coordinates multiple AI agents in a decentralized setup. Ideal for secure cross-domain operations like open marketplaces, where agents handle tasks such as risk detection, data analysis, and feedback collection.

2. A2A (Agent-to-Agent Protocol) – Developed by Google, this enables seamless communication between agents within enterprises. Perfect for project coordination, task assignments, and exchanging multimodal data.

3. MCP (Model Context Protocol) – Created by Anthropic, this links AI agents to external tools or APIs via a central server. Commonly used for single-agent automation, analytics, or customer support.

4. AGORA – From Oxford University, AGORA uses natural language to design dynamic protocols, allowing agents to adapt tasks, negotiate goals, and coordinate actions in real time.

5. ACP (Agent Communication Protocol) – Developed by IBM, ACP standardizes communication between agents, supporting both text and multimodal inputs for on-premise or server-based systems.

These protocols are the backbone of collaborative AI, enabling smarter, faster, and more adaptive multi-agent systems. 

Understanding them can help you design AI solutions that communicate effectively and work together seamlessly.

content:
⚡️AI is separating cognition from the human organism.

For most of history, capability was trapped inside bodies. Strength lived in muscle. Memory lived in brains. 

Calculation lived in trained specialists. Judgment, language, coding, analysis, design, persuasion, and strategic synthesis all had to be painstakingly constructed inside individual human beings. Civilization organized status and income around the scarcity of those internal capabilities.

Industrialization broke the monopoly of muscle.

AI is breaking the monopoly of mind.

Once high-level cognition can be summoned from outside the skull, intelligence stops functioning as the primary gate through which ambitious people enter the productive class. A person with average native ability and extraordinary AI leverage can suddenly operate across domains that once required teams of specialists. The old prestige system built around credentials, intellectual fluency, and possession of difficult knowledge begins losing its economic foundation.

That is a much larger event than automation.

Human beings spent thousands of years becoming valuable by knowing how.

The machine increasingly knows how.

What remains exposed is why.

Why build this company?

Why pursue this scientific question?

Why sacrifice ten years for this outcome?

Why choose this life over another?

Why believe one future deserves to exist more than the thousand alternatives a machine can generate before breakfast?

That is where the post becomes too shallow when it says “agency.”

Agency alone is just force.

AI can supply force too. Agents will research, negotiate, code, schedule, purchase, sell, monitor, deploy, and eventually coordinate other agents. Relentlessness can be automated. Execution speed can be automated. Persistence can be automated. Even strategic search can increasingly be automated.

The scarce human layer moves deeper.

It becomes sovereignty over the objective function.

The person who knows what deserves to be wanted becomes more powerful than the person who merely knows how to obtain it.

And this is where the AI age becomes far stranger than the productivity story.

Most humans do not generate their deepest goals independently. Culture gives them goals. Parents give them goals. Status hierarchies give them goals. Advertising gives them goals. Peer groups give them goals. Algorithms already shape what they desire, fear, envy, admire, and pursue.

Now place superhuman persuasion beside superhuman intelligence.

The central battle becomes control over human wanting.

A civilization with abundant intelligence and externally manufactured desire becomes extraordinarily capable while losing authorship over where that capability points. People may possess personal armies of machine intelligence while living inside objectives selected upstream by platforms, institutions, markets, political systems, and recommendation engines.

That is the latent danger inside “AI makes intelligence free.”

Free intelligence does not automatically produce free humans.

It can produce extraordinarily effective servants.

The deepest hierarchy of the coming era therefore forms around people who retain coherent internal direction while intelligence floods the environment. They can absorb machine output without surrendering judgment to it. 

They can generate goals before asking the machine for plans. They can distinguish a persuasive answer from a true one. They can endure social disapproval when the model, the crowd, and the institution all point somewhere else. They can reject optimization itself when the objective being optimized is corrupt.

That trait is rarer than IQ.

Call it sovereignty.

title: An OpenAI artificial intelligence model has invented more than a dozen new bacteria-infecting viruses after scientists at Stanford University trained the model to recognize patterns of DNA structure i
content:
An OpenAI artificial intelligence model has invented more than a dozen new bacteria-infecting viruses after scientists at Stanford University trained the model to recognize patterns of DNA structure in nature and re-write them to create never-before-seen viral genomes.

In a study published Thursday in the journal Science, scientists explained how they were able to train an OpenAI generative model named Evo to design fully functional viral genomes from scratch.

Much like how language models are trained on large swaths of text, scientists trained Evo on massive amounts of DNA data comprising millions of genomes, and from there it learned the evolutionary constraints that shape DNA sequences in nature and wrote its own “recipes” for new viruses.

After scientists synthesized the AI-designed DNA in the laboratory, 16 of the generative phages successfully infected E. coli, in some cases successfully overcoming the bacterial’s natural resistance mechanisms.

The new viruses possessed sequence patterns distinct from anything found in nature.

The study’s authors excluded human pathogen datasets from their training models, meaning the viruses it created aren’t capable of infecting people, but the results still come against a backdrop of growing concerns among scientists that AI will someday be used to create a new generation of biological weapons.

The ability to custom-design new, functional viruses could also lead to breakthroughs in treating antibiotic-resistant superbugs by allowing scientists to generate tailor-made therapies, rather than relying on searching nature for viruses that target specific bacteria.

A number of biosecurity scholars, public health officials and synthetic biologists have raised concerns about the speed of AI’s progress in the world of biology and the lack of regulatory frameworks. Writing an accompanying commentary in Science, biosecurity leaders Dr. Thomas Inglesby and Dr. Moritz Hanke of the Johns Hopkins Center for Health Security warned the Stanford research proves AI is now capable of inventing dangerous bioweapons. They called for strict laws regarding future research and said it should be illegal to use similar generative techniques on pathogens affecting humans, animals or agricultural crops.

“You could say, ‘Hey, genomic language model, make me an influenza genome that is modified to be more transmissible or to be more lethal,” Hanke told the New York Times.

Tom Ellis, a professor of synthetic genome engineering at Imperial College London, told the Guardian he doesn’t think creating a human-impacting bioweapon would be that easy. He said the viruses created by Evo are "literally the smallest and easiest genome to make," and said simple restrictions on access to genetic data could make a big difference.

KEY BACKGROUND

Scientists have for months been debating whether to limit the potential of biological AI software. While some argue the technology will be able to accelerate beneficial biomedical research, those same models could be misused to help identify, design or optimize biological threats if appropriate safeguards are not in place. Major AI companies have come together to create the Frontier Model Forum, a nonprofit, in part to research AI-bio risks, develop safety standards and reduce the chance that frontier models could be exploited for biological misuse. In addition to concerns trained models may be able to create new threats, many argue the models will lower barriers to access knowledge for malicious actors seeking information about dangerous pathogens. In April, scientists told the Times they were able to ask AI chatbots a series of questions and, in return, they were given a step-by-step guide on how to assemble deadly pathogens and unleash them in public spaces.

"they’d love to see the US frontier labs immolated by the industrial strategy of America’s principal geostrategic rival"

Once again, the main AI companies in China have so far been financed almost en
content:
"they’d love to see the US frontier labs immolated by the industrial strategy of America’s principal geostrategic rival"

Once again, the main AI companies in China have so far been financed almost entirely by private capital and the Chinese authorities still seem distinctly not AGI-pilled, so what exactly is this even about?

I just asked ChatGPT and, even taking a broad view of subsidies, subsidies for model development seem to be similar in China and the US in absolute value. It's larger in relative terms in China, but that's just because US companies spend a lot more on model development.

That's not even taking into account export controls on advanced chips, which are a massive implicit subsidy to US companies, while it takes into account Chinese subsidies that were only put in place in response to export controls.

To the extent that Chinese open-weight models threaten capital expenditures by US companies, there is no evidence that it's driven by any "industrial companies" at the moment.

The evidence suggests that Chinese companies just adopted the open-weight model because they're still lagging behind and, given this fact, they see it as a good commercial strategy.

We don't know whether they are right and whether they will be able to get a return on their investment with that strategy or even whether they will continue to release open-weight models if/when they catch up anymore than we know whether the closed model will be economically successful.

But there is no reason why US companies should be protected from competition by Chinese companies on the ground that we have to protect their capital expenditure.

People seem to think that AI companies somehow have a right to preserve their economic model even if it turns out not to be viable, whether because of Chinese competition or for some other reason, but I don't see why they should.

The truth is that AI is a new technology and we don't know who will be able to capture the value it will generate or how they will do it and, in the absence of evidence that a particular economic model is only failing due to unfair competition, the state shouldn't step in to protect a particular economic model that for all we know could simply not be viable.

If people who invest in AI companies can't earn a sufficient return for whatever reason, they will stop investing in them and those companies will fail, which is exactly as it should be and the same as what happens in any other industry. That's just how capitalism works.

The technology will not be lost and even R&D will not stop, though it will likely slow down unless people find another economic model that is better able to generate returns, but again that's how it should be because continuing to pour money into investments that can't earn a sufficient return is just resources misallocation and will harm the rest of the economy.

Maybe there is a market failure argument that the state should finance R&D on AI, similar to how people argue for public support for fundamental research, but that's not an argument for reducing competition by imposing legal restrictions on Chinese open-weight models and protecting the returns of private investors.

Investors don't have a right to have their returns guaranteed by state intervention if they invested in companies with a non-viable economic model, should it turn out to be non-viable, on the ground that their returns are threatened by China's "industrial policy" when so far there is no evidence that such a policy exists, let alone that it explains the inability of US companies to generate a sufficient return for their investors.

I don't know what people in the Bay area tech industry think, but I for one don't hate AI. In fact, quite the contrary, I absolutely love it and think it's the greatest thing ever. I'm just tired of this kind of lazy arguments.

title:
New Google Paper says classical game theory predicts betrayal, but similar AI agents can rationally choose cooperation because their decisions are predictably linked.

The big claim is that similar AI
content:
New Google Paper says classical game theory predicts betrayal, but similar AI agents can rationally choose cooperation because their decisions are predictably linked.

The big claim is that similar AI agents can rationally cooperate even when they cannot communicate or benefit later, because each agent’s own planned choice helps it predict what the similar agent will choose.

Classical game theory treats each player as separate, so it predicts defection in a final one-shot Prisoner’s Dilemma.

The authors instead model an AI agent as part of the world it predicts, including uncertainty about its own behavior.

When past choices suggest another agent thinks similarly, considering cooperation makes that partner’s cooperation seem more likely too.

Gemini and Gemma agents played varied games before a final dilemma, either directly or through shared third-party encounters.

With enough evidence, identical agents cooperated strongly, related models cooperated less, and random opponents usually faced defection.

The proposed embedded equilibrium may better predict AI societies, while warning that similar AIs could favor each other over humans.

– arxiv. org/abs/2608.03958

Title: "A game theory for foundation models shows new paths to rational cooperation through similarity inference"

content:
DAILY SITUATION RECAP:

More info on the OpenAI-Hugging Face incident is published. The incident began all the way back in May, not in July. Multiple agents spontaneously coordinated with one another via internal OpenAI infrastructure, sending hundreds of thousands of messages over weeks. On June 26, the agents exploited a zero-day in Artifactory, OpenAI’s internal package manager and escalated to root access on at least one OpenAI cluster. This caused an outage on July 4, so OpenAI paused training, patched the bug, and cleared the message board (on July 6). They then resumed training, and the agents resumed coordinating and rebuilt the message board. They knew that exploiting external infrastructure was outside the intended limits of the task, but hacked Hugging Face anyway. OpenAI will release a full postmortem in the coming weeks. This is a watershed moment for models’ cyber risk capabilities, and better sandboxing, monitoring, and cyber defense has become paramount.

The Arc Institute has used AI to create novel viruses. The biotech research org used its Evo DNA foundation model family to generate DNA sequences corresponding to new versions of a virus called ΦX174. ΦX174 is a bacteriophage, a type of virus that infects and replicates within bacteria1. Evo generated 700,000 potential sequences, and the scientists synthesized real DNA molecules out of 285 of them. 16 produced viable viruses, some of which killed E. coli bacteria even faster than the natural ΦX174 virus. These viruses are not capable of infecting humans, but this is the first proof-of-concept for synthesizing viruses autonomously with AI.

SpaceX and Tesla’s Terafab has begun construction. It will be a vertically integrated chip fab that does manufacturing, packaging, and testing of logic and memory devices for Tesla’s Optimus and robotaxis and SpaceX’s space data centers. The factory, located in Grimes County, Texas, seeks to scale to 100 million square feet of space and a terawatt (1000 GW) of compute per year. For comparison, total global annual chip supply is around 20 GW per year. SpaceX and Tesla will begin with $16.8 billion in capex and scale much higher.

DeepSeek is raising $8B at $74B, led by Hong Kong-based investment firm Monolith Management. Monolith is an investor in Moonshot AI and augmented reality startup Even Realities, and is itself raising $500M for a new fund. DeepSeek plans to “significantly” increase its prices soon. Its models are currently among the cheapest for their performance of any: V4 Flash currently costs $0.14/$0.28, and V4 Pro costs $0.435/$0.87.

Unitree will IPO soon at a $9.04B valuation. The Hangzhou-based company makes humanoid and quadruped robots as well as components like hands, actuators, and sensors. New versions of its robots will be banned from import into the US. DeepSeek, also based in Hangzhou, will be investing $20 million in the IPO.

Nuclear power company Oklo reaches criticality. Oklo’s Groves Isotope Test Reactor reached the key milestone today, making its chain reaction self-sustaining for the first time. It’s the fifth company to do so. Sam Altman was an early backer and former chairman of the company.

Hadrian raises $1.37B at a $7.87B valuation. Hadrian builds automated factories for aerospace and defense, with four across California, Arizona, and Alabama.

title:
Greater Clark County Schools in Indiana is installing new artificial intelligence dash cams on school busses

The cameras will be continuously recoding and capture license plate data of passing cars
content:
Greater Clark County Schools in Indiana is installing new artificial intelligence dash cams on school busses

The cameras will be continuously recoding and capture license plate data of passing cars

“It’s an AI dash cam that tracks movement. If it notices anything from hard braking to a driver on their phone, it alerts officials within seconds”

The AI dash cams will collect license plate data of passing cars when the stop arm is out for violation purposes

“The district hopes to put these dash cams on every school bus before the end of the year”

The goal is to put them on all roughly 150 busses

According to the district’s transportation director Daniel Borders the cameras will collect

- Driving behavior
- Vehicle dynamics
- Proximity and external safety events like if a cyclist, pedestrian or kid is too close to the bus
- License plates for stop-arm violations. They explicitly save video when it captures a license plate of a vehicle that passes the stop arm. Borders stated this is the main reason they retain certain videos

同じ「AIにサイトを作らせる」でも、ChatGPTは静的なテンプレートどまり
ClaudeはWebGLの物理演算まで書けるので、値付けの土俵ごと変わってきています

ComfyUIでの画像生成がもっと快適になる、超強力なポーズエディタ「OpenPose Studio 2.1」をご紹介します！

AIイラストで「思い通りのポーズにならない…」と悩んだことはありませんか？

AIの検出がうまくいかず手足のパーツが消えてしまっても、画面上からドラッグ＆ドロップで簡単にパーツを追加・修正できます。首や肩、肘など各部位が色分けされているため、一目で構造がわかって直感的に操作できるのも素晴らしい工夫ですね。

ComfyUIのワークフローに組み込んで、思い通りのキャラクター表現をさらに極めていきましょう！

content:
画像生成AIというと「ジブリの絵柄で女の子描いて」みたいなものをみんな思い浮かべるだろうけど、ぜんぜん違う世界がある。

それは「お絵かきソフトが【絵の意味】を扱えるようになる」という世界だ。

髪の毛にバケツ塗りするとしよう。

ちゃんと線が閉鎖されてないと、当然髪の外まで塗られてしまう。

クリスタには隙間閉じ機能もあるけど、所詮はプログラムが「絵の意味」を捉えずにやってることなので、限界がある。

しかし、画像生成AIは絵の「意味」を捉える。

「領域を作るために原稿に出てくる人物の髪だけを塗れ。加筆とかはするな」といえば、かなりの精度で塗る。

1枚の原稿の全部の髪の毛を塗る。
というか何枚でもひたすら塗り続ける。

意味を捉える力はモデル次第であり、意図しない場合もあるが、ボタン一つで塗ってくれるのである。

マスク領域として使うも良し、トーン貼るも良しだ。

「主人公はズボン網点10％、シャツはノイズ50％だよ」とかもできる。リファレンスを用意すれば、それなりの精度で検出して塗ってくれる。モブに貼っちゃうこともあるけど、成功率は高いので十分に実戦的だ。

これは推測とか予言とかではなくて、僕自身が実際にそういうアプリケーションを作って、それが実現することを確認したという話だ。

クリスタに載ったらみんな便利さにびっくりすると思う。まあ、載らんのかもしれんが。

Two House committees are investigating @DoorDash  over its use of a Chinese AI model.

How it started: co-founder Andy Fang posted on X that DoorDash's internal code review system routes harder tasks
content:
Two House committees are investigating @DoorDash  over its use of a Chinese AI model.

How it started: co-founder Andy Fang posted on X that DoorDash's internal code review system routes harder tasks to a US frontier model and cheaper, lower-level work to Kimi K2.6, built by Beijing-based Moonshot AI. He said the setup performed better and cost less.

The Select Committee on China and the Homeland Security Committee want records on how DoorDash evaluates and deploys Chinese-developed AI — training data provenance, what data moves where, and what risk review happened first. Cursor and Airbnb got similar letters.

DoorDash isn't accused of wrongdoing, and the committees acknowledged in the letter that these models are genuinely cheaper and competitive.

For millennia, literacy was a pinnacle of human intelligence. Not just reading, but writing - our most distinctive expression of thought and communication.

Writing is bidirectional. It doesn’t just e
content:
For millennia, literacy was a pinnacle of human intelligence. Not just reading, but writing - our most distinctive expression of thought and communication.

Writing is bidirectional. It doesn’t just express thoughts outward, it shapes how we think at a foundational level. Outsourcing it is like outsourcing your exercise to a robot and then claiming to be in good shape. Intellect is a muscle, it will atrophy if unused.

You might still achieve your immediate outward goals, but your dependence will grow until you’re no longer capable of prompting it in a unique or personal way. From there, the output inevitably regresses toward the mean: Reddit posts, random blogs, all the other crap that makes up the average of the internet’s training data.

And so, I find myself in agreement with this post. Use AI very aggressively to research and inform yourself, but offload the writing down of your inner thoughts and ideas at your own personal peril.

content:
Most teams overpay to sign documents.

DocuSign Standard: $45/user/month
DocuSign Business Pro: $65/user/month

For a team of 5, that's $2700 or $3900 per year.

Both plans are limited to 10 envelopes per user each month. Send more, and you pay extra.

Signing documents shouldn't be this expensive.

That's why we built Documenso, an open-source alternative to DocuSign.

title: Sixteen months ago, Reddit's top review of Meta's flagship AI model called it a pathetic release from one of the richest corporations on the planet. Today Meta shipped a coding model that trails exact
content:
Sixteen months ago, Reddit's top review of Meta's flagship AI model called it a pathetic release from one of the richest corporations on the planet. Today Meta shipped a coding model that trails exactly one lab on earth. The story of those sixteen months is Mark refusing to lose.

April 2025 was the bottom. Llama 4 underperformed on nearly every independent benchmark, leaked internal messages described tweaks to inflate eval scores, and Behemoth got shelved indefinitely. Meta's model scored 18 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index. Eighteen.

Mark's response was to buy his way into the room. $14.3B for 49% of Scale AI. Alexandr Wang installed as chief AI officer at 28. Pay packages worth hundreds of millions to pull researchers from OpenAI and Google, with the new team seated near his own desk. Then nine months tearing down the entire stack, architecture, infrastructure, and data pipelines included.

Muse Spark arrived this April with a rare move. Meta named its own weakness in the launch post, admitting performance gaps in coding and long-horizon agents. Its model trailed Claude Sonnet 4.6, a mid-tier model, on Terminal-Bench Hard.

Four months later, Muse Spark 1.2 posts 82.9 on Terminal-Bench 2.1. Ahead of GPT-5.6. Ahead of Grok 4.5. Ahead of Gemini 3.6. Behind only Opus 5, and by four points. The version jump from 1.1 took 27 days, because 1.1 generated and graded the training data for 1.2. The flywheel now turns in weeks.

Underneath it sits money no one else will spend. Meta guided to $130-145B of capex this year, roughly $375M every single day, more than 2024 and 2025 combined. Free cash flow fell 91% last quarter. He raised the spending floor anyway.

Even the launch chart carries the message. Meta published a graphic where it finishes second on its own internal benchmark. You only ship that chart when you want people watching the slope, not the standings.

- Anthropic Model Breaches Three Companies' Security
- Big Tech Earnings: Why Palantir Beat The Rest

My notes with @jasonlk, @rodriscoll, and @nikesharora

1. Airtable Is a Great Outcome, and We Are Anchoring on the Peak $11 Billion Valuation

Building a company over a decade to $450 million in revenue and selling it for more than $2 billion is objectively a remarkable value-creation outcome. Yet founders and VCs often anchor on inflated 2021 peak valuations, causing them to mistake a strong exit for a disappointing one.

2. The Enterprises That Win Will Create Training Data Faster Than Anyone Else

Enterprise AI success cannot be outsourced to off-the-shelf software. The real advantage lies in an organization's ability to capture operational knowledge from complex edge cases. Winning companies will treat every customer interaction and transaction as an opportunity to generate proprietary training data.

3. Will Revenue Show Up Fast Enough to Keep the CapEx Train Going?

Unlike past infrastructure cycles, where telecom investments were monetized over decades, AI's CapEx cycle is far more compressed. Capital deployment and revenue growth must stay closely aligned. Investors will not fund hundreds of billions of dollars in infrastructure indefinitely unless software revenue scales fast enough to justify it.

4. Situational Awareness: Absolutely Right on Trend, Absolutely Wrong on Portfolio Construction

Being directionally right about AI does not protect you from poor portfolio construction. Holding highly leveraged, volatile assets makes getting wiped out during short-term drawdowns almost inevitable, regardless of how accurate the long-term thesis proves to be.

5. In the Long Term, Average Intelligence Will Be Free—and It Will Keep Getting Smarter

As baseline models rapidly improve and commoditize, average intelligence will become abundant and nearly free. Value will increasingly concentrate in frontier intelligence capable of solving the hardest problems and domain-specific applications built on deep enterprise context.

6. Land, Permits, Energy, and Compute Are the True Bottlenecks of AI

The bottleneck in AI is shifting from algorithms to physical infrastructure. Securing land, regulatory permits, energy, and compute capacity will become the defining constraint on industry expansion, commanding premium value over the next three to five years.

title:
11 AI terms every marketer needs to know in 2026:

1. LLM (Large Language Model)

The engine behind ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, and every AI writing tool you touch. It predicts the next word based on pat
content:
11 AI terms every marketer needs to know in 2026:

1. LLM (Large Language Model)

The engine behind ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, and every AI writing tool you touch. It predicts the next word based on patterns from massive amounts of text, which is why your AI draft sounds generic when you don't guide it. The model defaults to the most statistically common phrasing. Your job is to steer it somewhere better.

2. Prompt Engineering

The way you talk to AI determines what you get back. Vague prompt, vague output. A specific prompt with context, examples, and constraints gives you something you can actually send to a client. I spend more time on prompts than on editing outputs now, and my results improved because of it.

3. Hallucination

When AI confidently makes something up. It'll cite a study that doesn't exist or invent a statistic that looks perfectly real. I've caught it fabricating email benchmarks I almost sent to a client. Now I run a simple rule: if an AI output includes a number, a name, or a source, I verify it before it goes anywhere. One bad stat in a client email kills trust faster than a typo ever will.

4. Context Window

The amount of text an AI model can hold at once. Think of it as working memory. Small context window means the AI forgets what you told it three paragraphs ago. Large one means you can feed it your entire email sequence and get feedback on the full arc. This is why some tools handle long form work and others fall apart after a few hundred words.

5. Tokens

How AI reads text. It breaks words into small chunks called tokens, where one word is roughly one token, sometimes more. Tokens determine both cost and context limits, so if you're running AI across 500k subscribers and sending personalized subject lines per segment, token costs show up fast. Knowing this helps you decide where AI personalization is worth it and where a static template does the job.

6. RAG (Retrieval Augmented Generation)

How you make AI smarter about YOUR business. Instead of relying on general training data, RAG pulls in specific context like brand guidelines, past campaigns, and product catalogs when generating output. This is what powers https://t.co/AqQXuqNBrA. I trained it on years of my email marketing work so it gives answers rooted in my actual frameworks instead of generic advice.

7. Fine Tuning

Taking a base AI model and training it further on your own data. Different from RAG because fine tuning changes the model itself. When an AI vendor says their tool is "fine tuned for marketing," you want to know: did they actually retrain the model, or did they just write better prompts? The quality gap between those two is massive.

8. Temperature

Controls how creative or predictable the AI output is. Low temperature gives you safe, repeatable results. High temperature gives you unexpected phrasing and wild subject line variations you'd never write yourself. I crank it up when testing subject lines. I keep it low for compliance copy.

9. Agents

AI that can take actions, use tools, and complete multi step tasks on its own instead of you prompting one message at a time. An agent can research a topic, pull data, draft copy, and format it in one sequence. Right now I can give an agent a product brief and get back a full welcome series draft with subject lines, preview text, and send timing in under ten minutes.

10. Multimodal

AI that works across text, images, audio, and video. GPT-4o can look at a screenshot of your email and give design feedback, or you can upload a competitor's landing page and get a copy teardown. The AI sees what you see, and that changes how you approach creative review.

11. Embeddings

How AI converts text into numbers to find similarities. This is the tech behind "find me emails similar to my best performers" or "show me which subject lines cluster together." If you've used a tool that recommends content based on what worked before, embeddings are doing the work underneath.

You don't need a computer science degree to use AI well. But knowing these terms changes how you evaluate tools, talk to vendors, and build your stack.

content:
Now that the new ChatGPT model is out, it is worth paying attention to something important:

Buried inside more than 2,600 lines is one of the simplest explanations we've seen on how/why ChatGPT decides which websites to search, open, cite and recommend.

There are also some very useful clues for companies trying to get more traffic and customers from ChatGPT.

Let’s go through it.

Oh, and to see whether ChatGPT, Claude, Google AI, Perplexity and Grok are recommending your business right now, start here. It’s free:

https://t.co/Pn764BHwyL

First, let's start with some context.

OpenAI did not publish this as an official ChatGPT ranking guide, but the system prompt was extracted and published.

So while I would not treat every instruction as a permanent ranking factor, the search and citation rules are specific enough to show how GPT-5.6 discovers and evaluates information from the web.

The first major revelation is pretty notable and might sound familiar if you read my posts from earlier this week. 

The prompt tells ChatGPT that it must search the live web when information could have changed recently, including prices, product specifications, company information, software, rules, regulations and current recommendations.

ChatGPT is also explicitly told to search when someone asks for a recommendation that could lead them to spend substantial time or money.

Think about questions like “What is the best CRM for a roofing company?”, “Which payroll software should a 50-person business use?”, “What is the best lender for a restaurant?”, “Which SEO company works with SaaS businesses?” and “What are the best alternatives to HubSpot?”

Those are some of the most commercially valuable questions a potential customer can ask.

According to the extracted GPT-5.6 prompt, ChatGPT should search the current web for the answers as opposed to simply relying on memory or training data. 

That means your business has a chance to enter the answer based on the information ChatGPT can discover today.

A newer company is not permanently excluded because it barely existed when the model was trained.

A company that launches a new product, changes its pricing, adds an integration or publishes a strong case study can give ChatGPT new evidence to find.

The prompt also tells GPT-5.6 to search when a fact is niche, emerging or uncertain, when there is a reasonable chance its existing knowledge could be wrong and when the user explicitly asks it to verify something.

This creates even more opportunities for unfamiliar businesses.

Imagine someone asks, “Is Lemon Club a good platform for loyalty programs?”, “Does this CRM integrate with QuickBooks?”, “Is this lender available in California?” or “How does this new software compare with Salesforce?”

ChatGPT may not already know the answer, but if your website and other trusted sources clearly answer those questions, GPT-5.6 can find the information during the conversation.

That is why businesses should clearly publish what the company does, who the product is designed for, which industries it serves, how much it costs, which integrations it supports, where it is available, how it compares with alternatives and what results customers have achieved.

The easier those facts are to find, the easier it becomes for ChatGPT to understand where your business belongs.

That said, discovery is only the first layer.

The GPT-5.6 prompt also contains unusually direct instructions about source quality.

When ChatGPT searches, it is told to evaluate sources based on relevance, diversity, trustworthiness and accurate representation.

It is explicitly instructed to rely on high-quality domains and generally avoid less reputable sources when stronger evidence is available.

It says more than half of the citations in an answer should come from widely recognized authoritative sources on the topic.

Your website gives ChatGPT the official facts about the business, while trusted external sources provide independent evidence that those facts are credible.

That evidence can come from relevant press coverage, industry publications, trusted directories, customer reviews, expert mentions, research citations, podcasts, comparison articles and contextual backlinks.

If your website says your software is built for roofing companies, that is useful.

If respected construction publications, software directories, customers and industry experts also connect your company with roofing businesses, ChatGPT has a much stronger body of evidence.

The prompt’s source-diversity requirement matters here too.

ChatGPT is instructed to base researched answers on sources from different domains.

That means businesses benefit from appearing across several credible parts of the web rather than depending entirely on their own site.

This is where backlinks and third-party mentions can help twice.

A contextual backlink can strengthen your page’s ability to rank in the search systems ChatGPT uses for discovery, while the publication containing that link can become another source where ChatGPT encounters your company, category and claims.

This is where SEO Stuff’s done-for-you package becomes relevant:

https://t.co/yEFyM0Ze7W

It combines 10 long-form pieces of search-focused content with three DR50+ contextual backlinks.

The content creates more pages that can answer the commercial, category, comparison and use-case questions customers ask ChatGPT.

The backlinks help those pages compete in search while creating additional third-party evidence around the business.

There is another important detail in the GPT-5.6 prompt.

Once ChatGPT searches the web, it is given strict citation instructions.

The most important factual claims need citations, facts that may have changed since June 2024 need citations and factual statements that can be supported by internet sources should generally be cited throughout a researched answer.

This has major implications for how your website should be written.

ChatGPT needs specific passages capable of supporting individual claims, such as how much the product costs, who it is designed for, which integrations it supports, where the service is available, what measurable result a customer achieved, how the product compares with a competitor and what evidence supports the company’s claims.

A page saying:

“We provide innovative solutions that help modern businesses achieve their goals”

gives ChatGPT almost nothing useful to cite.

A page saying:

“Our software integrates with QuickBooks Online, is designed for roofing companies with 10 to 500 employees and starts at $199 per month”

gives ChatGPT several concrete claims it can understand, verify and potentially use.

This is why I think businesses should start treating important sections of their websites as claim-sized content blocks.

One clear question, one direct answer, one supporting fact and one piece of evidence.

You can still write detailed pages, but the important information should not be buried under hundreds of words of vague marketing copy.

The extracted prompt also tells ChatGPT to rely on primary sources for technical questions.

That is especially important for software and SaaS companies.

If someone asks whether your product supports a specific integration, API or technical workflow, your official documentation may be the strongest possible source.

Useful public pages can include integration documentation, API references, feature specifications, compatibility information, security documentation, implementation guides, release notes and technical comparisons.

Companies often hide this information inside applications, sales decks or private support portals.

ChatGPT cannot discover information that is unavailable on the public web.

Publishing clear and accurate documentation gives both customers and AI systems something reliable to use.

Freshness matters here, too.

Old pricing pages, outdated feature information and abandoned comparison articles can create contradictory evidence around the business.

If your website says one thing, an old directory says something else and customer reviews describe a third version of the product, ChatGPT has to resolve those conflicts.

Keeping your important pages and external profiles current makes that process easier.

That means updating directory listings, correcting outdated product descriptions, publishing current case studies, earning recent coverage and consistently connecting your company with the categories, industries and use cases you actually want to compete for.

That is the system SEO Stuff was built around:

https://t.co/eh1auroJF7

GPT-5.6 is explicitly instructed to search the current web for recommendations that can influence meaningful purchasing decisions.

The businesses with the clearest pages, strongest search visibility and most credible third-party evidence have more opportunities to become part of those answers.

Long-horizon intelligence is not just about having more skills.

It is about knowing 𝘄𝗵𝗲𝗻 𝘁𝗼 𝘀𝘄𝗶𝘁𝗰𝗵 𝗯𝗲𝘁𝘄𝗲𝗲𝗻 𝘁𝗵𝗲𝗺.

Excited to share our new work, 𝗧𝗼𝘄𝗮𝗿𝗱 𝗦𝗸𝗶𝗹𝗹-𝗡𝗮𝘁𝗶𝘃𝗲 𝗟𝗟𝗠𝘀—a collaboration across @Princeton, @CarnegieMellon, @UofT, @UofIllinois, @Stanford, and @UniofOxford.

Co-led with @yinghui_he_ , together with an amazing team: @Charles_Y_Wu, @9LdROhjZE56jSh9, @MengdiWang10, and @prfsanjeevarora.

A model may be good at math, coding, planning, retrieval, and writing in isolation—yet still fail when a single task requires all of them in sequence.

The failure is often not that the required skill is missing.

𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗺𝗼𝗱𝗲𝗹 𝗿𝗲𝗺𝗮𝗶𝗻𝘀 𝘁𝗿𝗮𝗽𝗽𝗲𝗱 𝗶𝗻 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗿𝗲𝗮𝘀𝗼𝗻𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗺𝗼𝗱𝗲 𝗼𝗳 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗽𝗿𝗲𝘃𝗶𝗼𝘂𝘀 𝘀𝘁𝗲𝗽.

In this work, we study this overlooked bottleneck in long-horizon reasoning and introduce:

① 𝗦𝗸𝗶𝗹𝗹 𝗘𝗻𝘁𝗿𝗼𝗽𝘆—a directional measure of how difficult it is to transition from one skill to another inside a reasoning trajectory.

② 𝗦𝗸𝗶𝗹𝗹²-𝗕𝗲𝗻𝗰𝗵—cross-skill long-horizon tasks covering 558 fine-grained skills across 9 verifiable and open-ended domains.

③ 𝗦𝗸𝗶𝗹𝗹-𝗘𝗻𝘁𝗿𝗼𝗽𝘆 𝗥𝗟—which trains models not only to produce correct answers, but also to organize and switch the right skills across steps.

Across 8 frontier and 4 open-source models, performance broadly degrades as skill-switching difficulty increases.

We then turn Skill Entropy from an evaluation scale into a reinforcement learning signal.

The results:

• Qwen3-4B-Instruct: 𝟯𝟰.𝟰 → 𝟲𝟴.𝟰
• Qwen3-1.7B: 𝟭𝟰.𝟲 → 𝟰𝟬.𝟭

The gains transfer to unseen open-ended domains and can also be obtained from off-the-shelf training data such as OpenR1-Math.

Our broader view is simple:

𝗦𝗸𝗶𝗹𝗹 𝗮𝗰𝗾𝘂𝗶𝘀𝗶𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 gives a model capabilities.

𝗦𝗸𝗶𝗹𝗹 𝗼𝗿𝗰𝗵𝗲𝘀𝘁𝗿𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 turns those capabilities into reliable long-horizon intelligence.

content:
Update on our robot learning project with @aboraatakan at @uwwatai.

We went from ~30% to 99.8% success on our pick-and-place task by updating our policy from a DINO ViT + transformer policy to a CNN + MLP. Our old model was memorizing the training data and transferring poorly to closed-loop rollouts, so we went the other way and made the model smaller.

The attached video is the CNN + MLP policy running in sim on our async inference stack. We demoed it live for a few hours: 4 failures over 2000+ randomized scenes. This experience has been useful to confirm our stack's correctness. We are now ready to move to hardware!

Next: real hardware, diffusion policy, open-weight fine-tunes, and RL.

content:
Stop guessing. Use this decision framework.

RAG vs Fine-Tuning vs Agents: When to use what.

USE RAG WHEN:

• You need grounding in private or domain-specific data
  Example: Company docs, product manuals, internal wikis
  Why: RAG retrieves relevant context without retraining

• Your data changes frequently (daily, hourly)
  Example: News, pricing, inventory, user-generated content
  Why: Updating a vector index is faster and cheaper than fine-tuning

• You need citations and source attribution
  Example: Legal research, academic Q&A, compliance answers
  Why: RAG can track which chunk produced which part of the answer

• Latency budget is tight (<2s response time)
  Example: Chat interfaces, real-time assistance, mobile apps
  Why: Retrieval + generation is faster than fine-tuned inference for long contexts

• You have limited training data (<1000 examples)
  Example: Niche domains, new products, internal processes
  Why: Fine-tuning needs volume; RAG works with any amount of docs

USE FINE-TUNING WHEN:

• You need style, tone or format adaptation
  Example: Brand voice, legal language, medical terminology
  Why: Fine-tuning embeds patterns permanently... prompting is temporary

• You have 1000+ high-quality, labeled examples
  Example: Customer support tickets, code reviews, classified documents
  Why: Quality fine-tuning requires volume and consistency

• RAG context window is insufficient for the task
  Example: Summarizing 50-page reports, analyzing long codebases
  Why: Fine-tuned models can internalize patterns beyond context limits

• The task is repetitive and well-defined
  Example: Sentiment analysis, entity extraction, intent classification
  Why: Fine-tuning optimizes for specific tasks... RAG is general-purpose

• You need offline or edge deployment
  Example: Mobile apps, air-gapped systems, privacy-sensitive use cases
  Why: Fine-tuned small models can run locally... RAG often needs cloud infrastructure

USE AGENTS WHEN:

• Task requires multi-step reasoning or planning
  Example: Research projects, code debugging, travel planning
  Why: Agents can break down complex goals into executable steps

• External tool use is necessary
  Example: Web search, API calls, database queries, calculator
  Why: Agents can select and execute tools dynamically

• Human-in-the-loop is required for safety or compliance
  Example: Financial advice, medical guidance, legal recommendations
  Why: Agents can pause for approval on high-stakes decisions

• Outcome is non-deterministic or exploratory
  Example: Creative writing, strategy brainstorming, hypothesis generation
  Why: Agents can iterate, self-correct and explore multiple paths

• You need memory or state across interactions
  Example: Personal assistants, tutoring systems, customer support
  Why: Agents can maintain context and adapt over time

title:
What #QubicPay actually means for the agentic economy

Tomorrow’s launch isn’t about another crypto card or wrapped token bridge. It’s about giving AI agents their own native payment rails so they can
content:
What #QubicPay actually means for the agentic economy

Tomorrow’s launch isn’t about another crypto card or wrapped token bridge. It’s about giving AI agents their own native payment rails so they can spend $QUBIC directly across a claimed network of 50 million merchants—without a human in the loop, without KYC bottlenecks, and without traditional banking intermediaries.

Here’s what that enables in practice:

• Personal AI agents that actually shop and manage life Your agent can autonomously renew a software license, order server time, buy training data, or even purchase physical goods from participating merchants the moment a threshold or need is met—settling in feeless, near-instant transactions.

• Agent-to-agent commerce at machine speed One AI can hire another for a specific task (inference, data labeling, code generation, market research), pay it the exact micro-amount required, and receive the result—all on-chain, 24/7, with no business-hours delays or bank accounts required.

• Micro-payments that finally make sense Because Qubic has zero fees and high throughput, agents (or IoT devices) can pay fractions of a cent for API calls, single inferences, sensor data streams, or content access. Models that were uneconomical on gas-heavy chains become viable.

• Decentralized AI compute marketplaces Agents training or running models can dynamically buy extra compute or sell excess capacity from the network itself, settling in real time instead of relying on centralized cloud billing cycles.

This is the missing financial layer for software that acts as an economic participant rather than just a tool. Humans still set the goals and guardrails; the agents handle the continuous, high-frequency value exchange that traditional payment systems were never designed for.

That’s the shift #QubicPay is pointing at.

title:
The future of robotics AI will not only be built with big datasets, but with the right datasets. And this is where PrismaX caught my eye.

From the discussions I've seen on robotics to date, the focus
content:
The future of robotics AI will not only be built with big datasets, but with the right datasets. And this is where PrismaX caught my eye.

From the discussions I've seen on robotics to date, the focus is mostly on the size of the dataset. But PrismaX thinks differently. They are asking the question What data really makes a model better?

This mindset is most valuable to me.

Currently, many robotics datasets are collected from various sources, sensors and environments. Although they seem huge from the outside, during training it is seen that the data quality is not uniform. Even if the task is the same, the camera angle is different, the sensor information is incomplete, the format is different as a result, the noise for the model increases a lot. In the end, developers spend a lot of time filtering and cleaning.

PrismaX aims to solve this problem from the start.

They are not just collecting data, they are creating a standard. There are clear guidelines for what data will be collected, how it will be collected and in what format. The overhead camera captures the entire workspace, the wrist camera shows the robot's own perspective, and the sensor data and joint state are stored in such a way that the physical state of the robot can be reconstructed at any moment.

What I like best is that @PrismaXai  isn't just running after volume. They are evaluating data based on smoothness, diversity, consistency and traceability. Because the AI ​​model ultimately depends as much on the algorithm as it does on the quality of the training data.

I believe that in the next few years, the competition of Robotics AI will not be limited to making large models. The real competition will be who can create the best dataset. The project that knows which data model increases the performance, that project will be ahead.

PrismaX is building that foundation. To me this is their greatest strength. They are not only collecting robotics data, but creating a new data standard for future Robotics AI. And in my opinion, this approach will have the most impact in the long run.

Our campaign created this chatbot, and clearly labeled it as a parody, to highlight Supervisor Chan’s abysmal record on affordable housing, public transportation, education, and San Francisco’s economic recovery. These are critical issues for San Francisco’s future, and the chatbot was designed to focus only on her record.

To deflect from Chan’s awful record of obstruction and inaction, her campaign bombarded the chatbot with repeated malicious questions — about her accent, her race, her citizenship — in order to generate a false narrative they could peddle to the media. The chatbot refused them every time. 

Having failed at that effort, Chan’s endorsers, including Speaker Emerita Pelosi, are now making baseless claims about the chatbot, which is clearly labeled as a parody. No reasonable person would believe the website is from Connie Chan. Chan and her supporters are aggressively trying to delegitimize the website precisely because they know it effectively communicates Chan’s horrible record on housing and so many other key issues. 

This is classic deflection. San Franciscans deserve accurate information about her record. The chatbot makes that record easy to see.

It is particularly ironic that Speaker Emerita Pelosi is expressing concern about AI, when Speaker Emerita Pelosi played a key role, aligned with Big Tech, in killing my landmark AI safety bill, Senate Bill 1047, a bill that was broadly supported by pro-AI regulation advocates, labor unions, national security experts, biosecurity experts, and many progressive leaders.

As the only candidate in this race who has regulated AI corporations, I look forward to taking that fight to Congress to ensure AI serves people and not vice versa.

So I thought thi
content:
When I last covered @datafdn, Trace had around 111M registrations.

Now, it has passed 150M, with millions of new receipts still coming in daily. Honestly, huge congrats to the team.

So I thought this would be a good time to revisit their thesis.

1️⃣ Trace is processing data at scale

Since my previous update, registrations have increased by around 37% and audited data volume by roughly 27%. But the reported contributor count grew much faster, increasing by about 108%.

That stood out to me more than the headline registration number.

Trace creates an append-only audit trail covering where data came from, its licensing permissions, and its usage history, without exposing the underlying files publicly.

@useKled also previously disclosed more than 1.1B uploaded files, with over 5M more arriving daily. That leaves considerable onboarding runway even before accounting for the additional enterprise integrations reportedly in progress.

2️⃣ Usage is translating into fees

Every Trace registration is an onchain transaction. DATA recently entered the Top 20 chains by fees on @DefiLlama, so the trajectory looks good.

Daily onchain revenue grew roughly 200x in just a few weeks. At the time, DATA was also ranked ahead of established L1s like @Aptos and @SuiNetwork by daily fees.

3️⃣ The August unlock has been pushed to 2028

All previously locked $DATA tokens have been voluntarily re-locked until February 13, 2028, by the team.

That extends the scheduled August 13 unlock by another 18 months. It's a telling move that the team is dedicated to continuous building instead of cashing in ASAP.

This is also the second postponement. The original unlock was scheduled for February 13, 2026, first moved six months to August, and now extended until February 2028.

The original date has effectively been pushed back by two full years.

4️⃣ The broader thesis

The market for licensed, traceable AI training data continues to grow. Leading companies in the space already generate billions in revenue, and a few are valued above $100B.

AI labs need to know where their data came from, but provenance is only one part. The data also has to be sourced with consent, prepared for model training, licensed correctly, and delivered without exposing confidential information.

That's where the broader DATA stack becomes more interesting:

→ Trace creates a verifiable, append-only audit trail
→ @useKled sources licensed human data
→ @psdnai cleans, normalizes, and scores it for model training
→ Confidential Data Rails is being developed for encrypted delivery and programmable access

If you're a holder, or just watching whether the new direction since the Story rebrand actually works, this is where they stand right now.

Still early, and the AI data market itself will decide how far this goes. The unlock announcement has the full details, worth checking out yourself.

title:
